title: Figure's Robots Learn Any Home, UBTECH Scales to 10,000 Units, and Robots Get Their Own Ambulance
tldr: Figure AI's Helix 2.5 let humanoid robots do real chores in 30 homes they'd never seen before — a major leap in generalization.
UBTECH opened a plant designed to mass-produce humanoid robots at 10,000-unit scale, using robots to help build robots.
Agility's safety-certified Digit 5 humanoid landed $300M in orders ahead of a North America launch in early 2027.

news.body: Figure AI's Helix 2.5 model lets its humanoid robots walk into homes they've never seen and start working immediately. In a test across 30 unfamiliar homes, the robots tidied living rooms, folded and stored towels, and made beds with no prior mapping or training on that specific space.
news.means: Generalizing to unfamiliar environments has been the main thing keeping robots out of homes and small businesses — this is early evidence that barrier is breaking. Worth flagging to any client evaluating physical automation timelines.

news.body: UBTECH opened a plant built to manufacture humanoid robots at 10,000-unit scale — the first of its kind, using robots on the assembly line to help build more robots. Each unit gets over four hours of testing; UBTECH credits China's supply chain for making the scale possible. Separately, Goldman Sachs now projects 6.5M humanoid robots could ship globally by 2035.
news.means: A dedicated high-volume humanoid factory signals falling unit costs ahead. Useful context for client conversations about how soon humanoid labor becomes commercially viable rather than a pilot curiosity.

news.body: Agility Design's Digit 5 humanoid is built to work safely alongside people without barriers — it detects nearby humans and slows, stops, or powers down if approached. The company reports $300M in multiyear orders and plans a North America launch in early 2027, with Europe and the UK following later that year.
news.means: Real, paid orders for a safety-certified humanoid (not just a demo) is a concrete signal that industrial and warehouse clients are already buying, not only piloting. A good reference point if a client asks who's actually deploying these today.

news.body: Japanese company GMO unveiled a "humanoid ambulance" — a repair van stocked with diagnostic tools, spare parts, and a backup humanoid ready to swap in when a robot breaks down mid-shift, while engineers haul the broken unit back to base.
news.means: The maintenance and uptime layer is quietly becoming its own business line. If a client deploys robot labor, budget for a support/repair contract the same way they would for industrial equipment, not as an afterthought.
